basic.h2_when: When to use this two-number calculator
basic.p1: This page is built for fast, transparent arithmetic: you pick exactly one operation—add, subtract, multiply, or divide—and we apply it to the two numbers you type. That makes it easy to check homework, compare prices, or sanity-check a spreadsheet cell without dealing with full expression syntax.
basic.p2_afterExpr: . If you need standard order of operations (PEMDAS / BODMAS), use our
basic.p2_end: , which evaluate a full line of operators, parentheses, and functions.
basic.p3_prefix: Division by zero is rejected with a clear message. Negative inputs are allowed; the result follows the usual rules of arithmetic. If you specifically want “first minus second,” the
basic.p3_end: labels that pattern explicitly for word problems.
basic.p4_prefix: Results use JavaScript floating-point numbers—the same family of rounding quirks you see in spreadsheets. For money or grades, your teacher or employer may require a fixed number of decimal places; use the
basic.p4_end: after you compute a value if you need a documented rounding mode (including half-to-even “banker” rounding).
basic.p5: You can copy a short text summary or a shareable link from the toolbar when you want to send someone the same inputs—handy for tutors and study groups.

mean.avg_h2: When your worksheet says “average the scores”
mean.avg_p1: In many K–12 and intro college settings, “average” on a list of quiz or homework scores means the arithmetic mean: add every score, divide by how many there are. That is the number a gradebook or spreadsheet often shows as the class average when every assignment counts equally.
mean.avg_p2_prefix: This page uses that same definition. We also publish a
mean.avg_p2_end: with identical math—use whichever title your teacher or textbook prints in the instructions.
mean.stat_h2: Mean as a summary of a numeric dataset
mean.stat_p1: In statistics and data science, “mean” usually means the arithmetic mean: the balance point you get by spreading the total equally across every observation. It is sensitive to every value, which is a feature when you want a precise algebraic summary and a drawback when a few extreme points skew the story (think CEO pay mixed with typical salaries).
mean.stat_p2_prefix: If your syllabus uses the word “average” instead, open the
mean.stat_p2_end: —the calculation is the same; only the page framing differs for search and bookmarks.
mean.formula_p: Sum all entered numbers, then divide by the count. Scientific notation (e.g. 2e-3) parses like in a spreadsheet when JavaScript accepts it.
mean.outlier_h3: Outliers and when the mean misleads
mean.outlier_p_prefix: Every outlier pulls the mean toward it. If your data have a few extreme scores (housing prices, one very low exam in an otherwise strong term), the
mean.outlier_p_mid: often reports a more representative “center” than the mean. For “most common” values, use the
mean.lists_p: Separate numbers with commas, spaces, or semicolons. Scientific notation such as 1.5e3 is accepted where JavaScript parsing allows it. Empty or invalid tokens produce a clear validation message for accessibility and grading workflows.
